newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM's party votes, leader signals split.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM's party votes, leader signals split.

text.p: Leaders of Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's fractious party voted on Thursday to choose a president and struggled to patch up with its incumbent chief who signalled a bitter split in the ranks.
Leaders of the Janata Dal, the largest group in Gujral's 15-party United Front coalition, used the ballot box for the first time in the party's nine years to select their leaders.

But the dose of democracy, imposed by an activist Election Commission and supported by the Supreme Court, was obscured by party president Laloo Prasad Yadav's call to boycott the polls. Yadav alleged party voter lists had been rigged against him.
Results of the balloting in the main faction were not expected before Sunday.

A split in the party appeared a certainty on Thursday as Yadav, a low-caste leader and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, said his supporters would hold a convention in New Delhi on Saturday.
United News of India (UNI) said his supporters were busy thinking up a name for the group.
"I don't think we will succeed (in stopping a split). I participated in voting because it is my duty," said a government minister and Janata Dal leader who asked not to be identified.
"We are still trying, but hoping against hope," he said.
Laloo Yadav accused rival leaders of being rootless.
"I am the president and I will not tolerate these leaders who cannot (win) even five percent of the votes," UNI quoted him as saying in the state capital Patna.
Laloo Yadav's troubles in the party coincided with a corruption scandal which engulfed him and his party.
Yadav and 55 others have been indicted by federal police in a $280-million corruption case involving the alleged embezzlement of state animal husbandry funds.
Last month, the case forced a junior minister to resign from Gujral's two-month-old government. But Yadav, who says he is innocent, has refused to step down either as chief minister or party leader.

Gujral, who with other senior leaders has urged Yadav to quit, played down the split as he cast his vote at party headquarters in Delhi. "There could be differences of opinion and perception, but we all belong to one party," he said.
Former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda had veiled criticism for Yadav. "Some of the senior leaders want to avoid the election and they tried their best," he said.
The government minister told Reuters that Deve Gowda played a key role in angering Laloo Yadav by aiding his main contender, Sharad Yadav, who is also from Bihar but no relative of Yadav.
Federal Textiles Minister R.L. Jalappa, a critic of Deve Gowda, joined the boycott, the Press Trust of India said.
"It is clear that the dispute that is being witnessed in the Janata Dal is merely a feud between two factions," the Hindu newspaper said in an editorial.
Gujral has tried to keep above the fray for fear of being dragged into a fight that could weaken his grip on power.

Political analysts said Laloo Yadav was not expected to withdraw his crucial support to the centre-left alliance formed to counter the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), with vital support from the Congress party.
But continued tension in the coalition's main party would doubtless complicate Gurjal's task and could embolden its make-or-break ally, which offers support in a hung parliament.
